title: An old man hears a hymn
word: An old man hears a hymn
hook: past sixty, Amar Das hears Guru Angad's daughter Bibi Amro singing Nanak's words at dawn, and goes to find the Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, the akhara, the wrestling ground at Khadur. Your line was the body counts too. How did you move today? Day forty-eight.

Have you ever heard a song drift out of an open window and stopped walking? You didn't choose it. You weren't looking for it. It just found you. Here's a man who has been looking his whole life. His name is Amar Das. He's past sixty, a respected man in his village, and deeply devout. Tradition says he has walked to the Ganges on pilgrimage again and again, some say twenty times. He's done everything a devout man is supposed to do, and he still feels something missing. His nephew has married a young woman named Bibi Amro, who happens to be Guru Angad's daughter. And one morning before dawn, Amar Das hears her singing while she works. Today, the hymn that stopped him.
screen: `A SONG FROM AN OPEN WINDOW.` → `AMAR DAS, PAST SIXTY, STILL SEARCHING.` → `BIBI AMRO SINGS AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: She was singing a hymn of Guru Nanak's. Tradition doesn't agree on exactly which one, but the effect is the same in every telling. Amar Das stood still and listened, and then he asked her: whose words are those? My father's teacher, she said, Guru Nanak. And my father, Guru Angad, carries his light now, at Khadur. So an old man, a man of standing, got up and went to find a teacher about twenty-five years younger than himself. He bowed at Guru Angad's feet, and stayed. He would become the third Guru, and he wouldn't take up that role until his seventies. Notice a few things. First, who carried the hymn. Not a priest, not a scholar. A young woman singing while she did her morning work. The word traveled the way it was meant to, through ordinary people's voices, in their own language. That's what Guru Angad's letters and Mardana's rebab were for. Second, what the hymns are, on this path. Sikhs call the Gurus' words bani, and they treat bani itself as a teacher, as alive. A hymn heard at the right moment can change a whole life. And third, age. Amar Das had every reason to think his path was settled. He'd done the pilgrimages. He was old. Instead he started again as a beginner, and spent more than a decade learning to serve before anyone called him Guru. Sikhs tell his story to say that the door is open at any age, and it's never too late to hear something new.
screen: `WHOSE WORDS ARE THOSE?` · `AN OLD MAN BOWS TO A YOUNGER TEACHER.` · `BANI — THE WORD AS A LIVING TEACHER.` · `STARTING AGAIN AS A BEGINNER.` · then, large: `IT'S NEVER TOO LATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen closely to one song. Pick one now, any song, maybe one you haven't heard in years, or one someone you love used to sing. Close your eyes if you can. Listen to the words as if you're hearing them for the first time, like an old man stopped outside a window at dawn. Is there one line in it you never really heard before? The bell holds the time.
An old man hears a hymn. Amar Das, past sixty, stopped by Bibi Amro's dawn singing, who went to find Guru Angad and became the third Guru. Today's word.
screen: `AN OLD MAN HEARS A HYMN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it's never too late. Today, start one small thing you told yourself you were too old for. Day forty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Amar Das as the third Guru and tell of Bibi Amro's singing as the moment that brought him to Guru Angad; many Sikhs begin the day by reciting or listening to the Gurus' hymns before dawn.

fork.setup: you're past sixty and respected, and you've done every pilgrimage. at dawn you hear a hymn that stops you cold. what do you do?
options: enjoy it and go on with your day.
find out whose words they are, and go to that teacher.
decide you're too old to change paths.
fork.reveal: Amar Das asked Bibi Amro whose words they were, and went to Khadur to bow before a Guru much younger than himself.

original.note: Gurmukhi: bani, the word; for Sikhs, the Gurus' hymns, treated as a living teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man liked a song.
what it means: a lifelong seeker finds his teacher through a hymn sung by an ordinary young woman, and starts over as a beginner.
what a scholar hears: tradition places this around 1540, with Amar Das about sixty-one; he became the third Guru in 1552, in his early seventies.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition (Bibi Amro and Amar Das)
Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 46 (Guru Amar Das)

notes: Amar Das's birth (1479) and succession (1552, aged about 73); meeting Guru Angad about 1540 (aged about 61). Confirm.
'Some say twenty' pilgrimages to the Ganges/Haridwar: common tradition; confirm.
Bibi Amro married to Amar Das's nephew (his brother's son): confirm.
Which hymn she sang is disputed (often given as a Maru or Sri Raag hymn of Guru Nanak); script says tradition doesn't agree. Confirm.
Age gap 'about twenty-five years' (Angad born 1504): confirm.
